title: A thrift stop for the cats.
summary: A family thrift stop at Safe Haven in Wells, with a $1 L.L.Bean find, a vintage school-dance shirt recommendation and a free board for future browsing.
search: Safe Haven · Wells, Maine A thrift stop for the cats. Our favorite $1 L.L.Bean find, a vintage Tommy Jeans velour shirt for James’s upcoming school dance, and a fellow thrifter’s directions to the clearance walls. A family stop at Safe Haven in Wells, with practical notes and a free board for a future browse. October 18, 2026 · From the family camera roll A Sunday stop at Safe Haven, with autumn flowers by the door. Our favorite find at Safe Haven in Wells was L.L.Bean for $1. We also met a lovely, inveterate thrifter who recommended a vintage Tommy Jeans velour shirt for James, with his upcoming school dance in mind. Retro cool was the idea. He told us Safe Haven was the absolute best store he goes to, then pointed out the $1 clearance walls along the side and back of the store. That is the sort of recommendation I like: directions to the dollar section and an eye for a school-dance shirt. Our October camera roll has plenty else to look at. Floral lamps in a sunny window. Wicker chairs. A patchwork quilt draped over a wooden stand. Baskets, cushions, old records and shelves that reward a second look. This is a shop with quite a lot going on. The lamps and wicker department, making a case for looking closely.Quilts, cushions, baskets—and quite a few possible distractions. The antiques continue upstairs. In our photographs, a large lighted Christmas tree stands beside the wooden staircase. The flowers outside are still firmly in October; the tree has started work early. And then there is the sign on the door: Don’t let the cats out, no matter what they tell you! A very clear instruction, with room for the possibility that the cats have prepared an argument. The cats are the reason behind the shopping. Safe Haven says proceeds from its Vintage/Thrift/Antique Shop at Cattail Farm help fund its all-volunteer cat rescue, rehabilitation, adoption and care work in York County. A useful place to browse, with a purpose beyond the next set of shelves. A tip passed along in the shopAsk about the $1 clearance walls.A fellow shopper pointed us to the clearance walls along the side and back of the store. Ask which areas are marked $1, then check each item’s label.For a clothing browse, check size, care instructions, seams and fastenings before deciding. Prices and stock change; not everything in the shop is $1. The practical partA little looking, with the route in mind. The photographs show the browsing spaces and the stairs we used. Here are the details another family may want before deciding how much of the shop to explore. The photographed route to the upstairs antiques has wooden stairs and handrails. What we can show you Antiques upstairsThe sign directs shoppers up a wooden staircase. We have not confirmed a lift or another step-free way to reach that area. Ask what can be browsed on the entrance level if stairs do not work for your visit. Closely arranged displaysFurniture, baskets and breakable items sit close together in some photographed areas. We have not measured aisle widths or turning space. Ask about the route for a wheelchair, walker or stroller before relying on it. Arrival and a place to pauseThe exterior photographs show asphalt in front of the shop, with merchandise near the entrance. They do not establish a complete step-free route, accessible parking or a usable restroom. Confirm the details you need and choose a place to pause with your group. Light and the amount to look atOur photos show sunny windows, overhead lights, a lighted display tree and plenty of merchandise. Sound levels and busy periods were not recorded. If the $1 section is the goal, ask where it is and check the labels. There is no requirement to buy something or visit every floor. These notes are for adult siblings, including siblings who have disabilities themselves. They do not presume closeness or a particular caring arrangement. Keep the volume and equipment comfortable for the person using them. The short snack run Agree the place, order, support and way home before leaving. One familiar stop is enough. Check any current eating arrangements, and do not turn ordering into an unexpected test of independence. A takeaway brought to the house can be the smaller version when travel is too much. The shared episode, game or interest Pick something both people actually enjoy. Decide whether this is a whole episode, a few minutes, watching someone else play or simply being in the same room. Keep a clear way to pause. Participation need not look equal every minute for the time to feel shared. Say what you are agreeing to.+If you offer practical help, name the job and its limits. “I can bring dinner on Thursday” does not quietly become “I can cover the evening.” If a visit includes sole support, agree that separately and make sure you have the knowledge, ability and backup it requires. Time: when you are available and when you need to leave.Responsibility: the exact task you are taking on.Preparation: what you need to learn or receive beforehand.Changes: who is contacted if the plan cannot go ahead. A useful sentence is: “I can handle the library visit once a month if the transport and handover are arranged. I cannot be the last-minute backup.” The wording can stay kind and direct. Talk about the future before it becomes an emergency.+Begin with what your sibling wants for their own life. Use the communication supports they need to take part. Then ask family members which responsibilities they are willing and able to accept. The Sibling Leadership Network’s future-planning resources provide a starting point for these wider conversations. For a first meeting, choose one question: who knows the current support arrangements, where useful records are kept, or which people your sibling wants involved. End with one next step and a named person who has agreed to it. Nobody needs to promise a lifetime of support in a single conversation. Keep formal questions about finances, benefits, housing, decision-making authority and legal documents with qualified advisers and the relevant service providers. A family conversation can identify a gap; this guide cannot settle those arrangements. Give each other room to be adults.+Ask before taking or sharing photographs, retelling private stories or adding someone to a family message thread. Speak directly to your sibling rather than conducting every conversation through a parent. Ask what help is welcome instead of assuming your preferred solution is theirs. For younger siblings in the family, keep ordinary sibling time separate from adult care responsibilities. An older child’s availability is not a substitute for the support the adults have agreed to provide. A small arrangement that travels well.+From farther away, offer a specific recurring connection if you want one: a short Sunday call, choosing the next film, a birthday card or a visit planned well ahead. Check whether the format works for your sibling and who, if anyone, has agreed to help make it happen. Finish a visit with a clear goodbye and a realistic next plan. “I will text about next month” is better than promising every Saturday when your calendar cannot support it.
